chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Main Types of Real Estate

lessons.title: Land as an Investment: Agricultural, Non-Agricultural and Conversion Risk

children.text: "Buy land, they are not making any more of it." It is the oldest property advice in India, and it has made some families very rich. It has also trapped others in land they cannot legally own, cannot build on and cannot sell. The difference is rarely the soil. It is the paperwork: what the land is allowed to be used for, and who is allowed to buy it. This lesson teaches you to see land the way a developer or property lawyer does.

body.text: When you buy land, you are really buying a set of legal permissions: what it can be used for and who can own it. Change those permissions and the same acre can be worth several times more, or become almost impossible to sell.

children.text: Two Legal Worlds: Agricultural and Non-Agricultural Land

markDefs.definition: Land that revenue records permit to be used only for farming and related activities.
Land legally permitted for residential, commercial or industrial use, often called NA land in western and southern India.
A statutory plan prepared by a city or regional planning authority that divides land into zones such as residential, commercial, industrial, green or agricultural.

children.text: In Indian law, land falls into two broad buckets.
Agricultural land
can be used only for farming.
Non-agricultural (NA) land

can be used for homes, shops, offices or factories. Land is a state subject under the Constitution, so every state writes its own rules, and what is permitted on a particular piece of land also depends on the local
development plan

children.text: Who Is Allowed to Buy Agricultural Land?
This is the rule that catches most city investors. Many states protect farmland by limiting who can own it. Buying in breach of these rules can make the sale void, no matter how much you paid.

body.caption: Agricultural land purchase rules: examples
headers: What it means for an investor

cells: Under the Maharashtra Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, a non-agriculturist generally cannot buy agricultural land
A salaried Mumbai or Pune resident usually cannot buy farmland directly
Purchase is generally limited to people who are farmers
Farmer status must be proven, and claims are scrutinised
A 2020 amendment removed the old income and farmer restrictions
Open for now, but the state has announced an intention to restore restrictions
Non-agriculturists need state government permission to buy land
Holiday-home and orchard buyers face a permission process
NRIs and OCIs, anywhere in India
Cannot buy agricultural land, plantation property or farmhouses under FEMA rules
They can inherit such land, but not purchase it

body.text: Brokers have workarounds for these rules, and most of them are dangerous. "We will get you a farmer certificate," "register it in a local farmer's name," or "take a power of attorney now and do the sale deed later" can all leave you with no legal title. In Suraj Lamps and Industries v State of Haryana (2011), the Supreme Court held that sales through a general power of attorney, an agreement to sell or a will do not transfer ownership. Only a registered sale deed does.

body.title: The NRI question
body.question: Ramesh is an NRI working in Dubai. Which of these can he legally do under FEMA rules?
options: Buy 5 acres of farmland in Kerala in his own name
Inherit agricultural land from his father in Punjab
Buy a tea plantation in Assam
body.explanation: NRIs and OCIs cannot purchase agricultural land, farmhouses or plantation property in India, but they can inherit them. They are free to buy residential and commercial property.

children.text: Conversion: Where Land Values Multiply

markDefs.definition: The legal process of changing land's permitted use from agricultural to residential, commercial or industrial, usually on payment of a fee or premium to the state.

children.text: The biggest price jumps in Indian real estate happen when agricultural land gets
converted
to non-agricultural use and then turned into an approved layout. Each step unlocks value, and each step carries approval risk.
Check the zone.
Is the land in a residential, industrial or green zone in the development or regional plan? Conversion is realistic only where the plan permits the new use.
Apply for conversion.
Typically to the district collector or revenue department, with title documents, survey maps and no-objection certificates.
Pay the fee or premium.
Usually linked to the land's area and its government-assessed value.
Get the layout approved.
The planning authority sanctions roads, open spaces and plot sizes, and a good share of the land goes to roads, parks and civic amenities.
Develop and sell.
Build roads, drainage, water and power lines, register with RERA where required, and sell individual plots.

body.label: Maharashtra's 2025 conversion reform
body.value: No separate NA permission where the use is already allowed
body.context: The Maharashtra Land Revenue Code (Second Amendment) Act, 2025 treats an approved building plan as deemed NA permission where the development or regional plan permits the use, and replaces the annual NA tax with a one-time conversion premium. Land outside such zones still faces conversion hurdles.

body.title: How one acre's value can grow through conversion (illustrative, ₹ lakh)

data.label: Plots sold at ₹3,000 per sq ft

body.caption: 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft. After roads, parks and civic amenities, often only about 55% to 60% of a layout is sold as plots.

body.title: Show me the math for the chart

children.text: One acre = 43,560 sq ft
Saleable area at 60%: 43,560 × 0.60 = 26,136 sq ft
Gross plot sales at ₹3,000 per sq ft: 26,136 × ₹3,000 = ₹7,84,08,000, or about ₹784 lakh

The jump from ₹80 lakh to ₹784 lakh is not profit. It has to pay for conversion premiums, approvals, roads, drainage, power, marketing, interest and years of waiting, plus the risk that approvals never come.

body.title: Size up a layout
body.prompt: A developer holds 2 acres near Hoskote, Bengaluru. After roads and parks, 55% of the land can be sold as plots at ₹2,500 per sq ft. What are the gross plot sales, in ₹ crore? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 2 acres = 87,120 sq ft. Saleable area = 87,120 × 0.55 = 47,916 sq ft. Gross sales = 47,916 × ₹2,500 = ₹11,97,90,000, or about ₹11.98 crore. Development costs, approvals, interest and time all come out of this figure.

body.text: Who captures that conversion value? Mostly developers and patient landowners who can fund approvals, infrastructure and delays. Small investors are usually sold land at a price that already assumes conversion will happen, sometimes marketed as "future NA" or "near the upcoming airport." If the conversion or the infrastructure is delayed by five years, they carry all of the risk and none of the control.

children.text: Reading Land Records

markDefs.definition: The updating of revenue records to show a new owner after a sale, inheritance or gift. Mutation records ownership for revenue purposes but does not by itself prove title.

children.text: Every state maintains revenue records showing who holds a piece of land, its area, its classification and its crop history. Each state calls these records something different, and most now let you view them online. They are your starting point for any land check, together with
mutation
entries showing how ownership changed over time.

body.title: The tax twist: when agricultural land is not a capital asset

children.text: Indian income tax law treats rural agricultural land differently from urban land. Agricultural land that lies outside municipal limits, and beyond a specified distance from them, is not a capital asset, so gains on selling it are not taxed as capital gains. The distance depends on the town's population:

content.caption: Agricultural land treated as a capital asset (urban agricultural land)
headers: Population of the municipality or cantonment
Land counts as a capital asset if it is within

cells: More than 10,000 but up to 1 lakh
More than 1 lakh but up to 10 lakh

children.text: Distances are measured aerially. Land just outside these boundaries can be sold without capital gains tax; land just inside cannot. Always confirm the position with a tax professional, since the treatment depends on exact location and current law.

body.title: Pramod's farmland near the expressway
body.scenario: Pramod, a salaried IT manager in Pune with no family farming background, is offered 2 acres of agricultural land in Nashik district for ₹60 lakh, close to an interchange on the Samruddhi Mahamarg. The broker says: "Take a power of attorney and agreement now. The 7/12 will be transferred later. Once it becomes NA, it will be worth ₹3 crore."
body.prompt: What legal and investment problems should Pramod think through?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Eligibility: Maharashtra generally bars non-agriculturists from buying agricultural land. Without proven agriculturist status, a direct purchase may be invalid.
2. No real title: after Suraj Lamps (2011), a power of attorney and agreement to sell do not transfer ownership. Pramod would have paid ₹60 lakh without owning the land.
3. "Later" may never come: if the 7/12 cannot legally be transferred to him, the seller or their heirs can still deal with the land.
4. Conversion is not automatic: Maharashtra's 2025 reform helps only where the development or regional plan permits non-agricultural use. Pramod must check the zoning of this exact survey number.
5. The ₹3 crore figure is a guess: it assumes conversion, infrastructure-led demand and a buyer at that price. None of these are guaranteed.
6. Title checks: he would need the full 7/12 history, mutation entries, consent of all legal heirs and an encumbrance search.
7. Holding reality: no income, possible encroachment, and a narrow market of buyers who can legally purchase agricultural land.
8. Safer alternative: if he wants land exposure, an approved, converted plot with clean title, or listed real estate routes, avoids most of these legal traps.

body.title: Land Due Diligence Before You Pay a Token Amount
steps: Confirm you are legally eligible to buy this category of land in this state
Pull the current land record (7/12, RTC, Patta, Khatauni) and at least 30 years of ownership history
Check mutation entries and confirm all legal heirs are signing the sale
Verify the zoning in the development or regional plan for the exact survey number
Get an encumbrance certificate to check for loans or charges on the land
Walk the boundaries with a licensed surveyor and compare them with survey maps
Insist on a registered sale deed, never a power of attorney or agreement alone
Have a qualified property lawyer review everything before paying

points: Land value depends on legal permissions: what the land can be used for and who can own it.
Agricultural land is cheaper but restricted: several states limit buyers, and NRIs and OCIs cannot purchase it at all.
Conversion and approved layouts can multiply value per acre, but costs, delays and approval risk absorb much of that jump.
Maharashtra's 2025 reform removes separate NA permission only where the development plan already permits the use.
A power of attorney or agreement to sell does not transfer ownership; only a registered sale deed does.
Check land records, mutation history, zoning, encumbrances and all legal heirs before paying anything.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. Land laws differ by state and change often, and the state examples here are simplified. Always verify eligibility, title and zoning with a qualified property lawyer, confirm tax treatment with a tax professional, and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
